sprints.2: Sprint 2 — Securing and Limiting an AI Service
sprints.4: Sprint 4 — Project: AI Service with Companion UI

campus.title: What an AI Service Is
campus.outcome: Distinguish an AI application (used directly) from an AI service (called by other systems) and explain why the difference matters for design choices.

campus.title: What an AI Service Is
campus.outcome: Explain REST endpoints, HTTP methods, and status codes at the level needed to understand and configure an AI service — not to design an API from scratch.

campus.title: Working with a Service Scaffold
campus.outcome: Tour the provided FastAPI scaffold that wraps a Module A-style application; identify the routes, inputs, outputs, and where the model is called.

campus.title: Working with a Service Scaffold
campus.sublesson: Extending the scaffold for a new use case
campus.outcome: Extend the provided scaffold by adding a new endpoint that calls the model with a different prompt — focused on configuration, not authoring from scratch.

campus.title: Input and Output Contracts
campus.sublesson: Why contracts matter for AI services
campus.outcome: Explain why downstream systems need predictable inputs and outputs and how validation prevents whole categories of failure.

campus.title: Versioning AI Endpoints
campus.sublesson: Why and how to version AI endpoints
campus.outcome: Apply endpoint versioning (/v1, /v2) so model and prompt changes can be deployed and deprecated independently.

campus.title: Sprint 1 Assessment
campus.outcome: Extend the provided service scaffold with one new endpoint, define its input/output contract, and version the route.

campus.title: Authenticating an AI Service
campus.outcome: Explain what API key authentication does, why AI services need it, and where the keys live.

campus.title: Authenticating an AI Service
campus.sublesson: Adding API key auth to the scaffold
campus.outcome: Apply API key authentication to the provided service scaffold using a provided pattern.

campus.title: Secrets Management
campus.sublesson: What is a secret and where it should live
campus.outcome: Define which values count as secrets, where they should and should not live, and the most common ways they get leaked — including logs, prompts, and version control.

campus.title: Rate Limiting
campus.sublesson: Why AI services need rate limits
campus.outcome: Explain why AI services need rate limits — cost, abuse, fairness — and the common patterns (per-key, per-endpoint, per-IP).

campus.title: Rate Limiting
campus.outcome: Apply per-key rate limiting on the service scaffold and observe behavior under burst traffic.

campus.title: Sprint 2 Assessment
campus.outcome: Apply API key auth, environment-based secrets, and per-key rate limiting to the project service.

campus.title: Streaming Responses
campus.outcome: Explain when streaming improves user experience for AI endpoints and when it is unnecessary complexity.

campus.title: Streaming Responses
campus.outcome: Enable streaming on the provided service scaffold and observe the difference from the client side.

campus.title: Observability for AI Services
campus.outcome: Identify the signals worth logging — request IDs, model used, tokens, latency, errors — and why each matters for debugging and cost tracking.

campus.title: Observability for AI Services
campus.outcome: Identify content that should not be logged (personal data, sensitive prompts, full secrets) and apply provided redaction patterns.

campus.title: Service Logs as Evaluation Feedback
campus.sublesson: Closing the loop with existing evaluation
campus.outcome: Use service logs as a feedback signal into the evaluation framework introduced in Module A — extending existing eval work rather than building a new framework.

campus.title: Sprint 3 Assessment
campus.outcome: Enable streaming, add structured logging with redaction, and connect logs back into the existing evaluation framework from Module A.

campus.title: Companion UI via Vibe Coding
campus.sublesson: Scoped companion UI using Lovable + Supabase
campus.outcome: Use a vibe coding tool (Lovable or Bolt.new) to build a minimal companion UI on top of the project service. Lovable uses Supabase as its built-in backend — no separate Supabase setup required. Required scope: one input form, one response display, one logged interaction. Auth and streaming use provided patterns; richer dashboards are explicit extension tasks, not required for credit.

campus.title: Companion UI via Vibe Coding
campus.sublesson: Connecting the UI to the service
campus.outcome: Wire the scoped vibe-coded UI to the project service endpoints using provided auth and streaming patterns.

campus.title: End-to-End Testing
campus.outcome: Run manual end-to-end tests across the UI → service → model path and document integration failures.

campus.title: Documentation
campus.outcome: Write a README and basic API documentation so another team member could call and understand the service.
